title: Not ashamed (Romans 1:16)
hook: the gospel is the power of God unto salvation

segments.voice: Yesterday, how Paul wrote: dictated letters, signed in big handwriting. Your line was real letters to real people. Did you write a few lines to someone? Day five hundred sixty.

Most of us know the small hesitation. You're at a restaurant with coworkers and you wonder whether to make the sign of the cross before you eat. Someone asks what you did on Sunday and you say, oh, not much. Nobody is persecuting you. It's just easier not to mention it. Paul knew that feeling well, and in the letter that opens the New Testament's collection of letters, he answers it in the first chapter.
screen: `THE SIGN OF THE CROSS AT LUNCH?` → `OH, NOT MUCH.` → `PAUL KNEW THAT FEELING.`

segments.voice: Romans is a letter to a church Paul had not founded and had never visited. He's writing ahead, probably from Corinth, introducing himself and his message before he arrives. And though Romans comes first among the letters in your Bible, it isn't the oldest. Paul's letters are arranged roughly by length, longest first. Romans is simply the longest. Near the start, Paul says what the whole letter is about. In the King James: "For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek." Why would he even mention shame? Because in his world, his message was embarrassing. Crucifixion was the most shameful death Rome had, reserved for slaves and rebels. To say that God's anointed one died on a cross sounded, to many people, ridiculous. And Rome was the capital of honor and power. Paul is about to write to the people at the center of that world, and he begins: I'm not ashamed of this. Notice what he calls the gospel: not an idea or an argument, but power, the Greek word dunamis, the root of our word dynamite. And notice who it's for: everyone who believes, Jew first and also Greek, no one shut out. Catholics have long used a small gesture for this very thing. Before the Gospel at Mass, they trace a small cross on the forehead, lips and heart, as if to say: in my mind, on my lips, in my heart, unashamed.
screen: `A LETTER TO A CHURCH HE'D NEVER SEEN.` · `FIRST IN ORDER, NOT FIRST WRITTEN.` · `A SHAMEFUL DEATH, AN EMBARRASSING MESSAGE.` · `POWER, NOT JUST AN IDEA.` · then, large: `I AM NOT ASHAMED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say grace in public, if you pray. Settle, and breathe. Think of your next meal with other people around, at work, in a restaurant, in a school cafeteria. Picture yourself pausing before you eat. Maybe a sign of the cross. Maybe a few silent words. Maybe just a moment of thanks, eyes open. Notice what you feel imagining it: a flush of self-consciousness, maybe. That's normal. Paul felt the pull too. If grace isn't your practice, picture simply being honest about something you care about, when it would be easier to say not much. The bell holds the time.
Not ashamed. Paul's opening claim to Rome: the gospel of a crucified Messiah is the power of God for everyone who believes. Today's word.

Your line: not ashamed. Today, at one meal, pause and give thanks where others can see. And that's week eighty: more blessed to give, arrested, almost, shipwreck, Rome, epistle, and not ashamed. Day five hundred sixty.

howItsDone: Many Catholics make the sign of the cross and say grace before meals, including in public, and at Mass they trace a small cross on the forehead, lips and heart before the Gospel is read.

fork.setup: you're Paul, writing to Christians in Rome, the capital of honor and power. your message centers on a man executed on a cross. how do you open?
options: play down the cross and stress his teaching.
say plainly you're not ashamed of it.
save the hard part for a visit.
fork.reveal: he names the shame head on: I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth.

original.note: Greek: to be ashamed of. Paul says, ou gar epaischynomai, for I am not ashamed.

trapdoor: what you thought: not ashamed means being bold about religion.
what it means: in a world where crucifixion meant total disgrace, Paul says the message of a crucified Messiah is God's own power.
what a scholar hears: Romans 1:16–17 is often read as the theme of the whole letter. the word for power, dunamis, gave us dynamite, a name Alfred Nobel took from the Greek.

Pauline letters ordered roughly by decreasing length: standard; confirm.
